Stott opens the Titus half of the volume with the letter's main themes, doctrine and duty, and reads the opening greeting (1:1-4) in that light: Paul's apostleship serves the faith of God's people and their knowledge of the truth that leads to godliness.
The letter's main themes and opening

Ver. 1. "Paul, a servant of God, and an Apostle of Jesus Christ, according to the faith of God's elect." You observe how he uses these expressions indifferently, sometimes calling himself the "servant of God," and sometimes the "servant of Christ," thus making no difference between the Father and the Son. "According to the faith of God's elect, and the acknowledging of the truth which is after godliness.
2: Reads eternal life as the life of God himself given to believers, begun now and finished later, and says this hope rests on a promise from a God who cannot lie, not on wishful thinking.
An apostle in the hope of eternal life

Ver. 2. "Which God, that cannot lie, promised before the world began." That is, not now upon a change of mind, but from the beginning it was so foreordained. This he often asserts, as when he says, "Separated unto the Gospel of God." (Rom. i. 1.) And again, "Whom He did foreknow, He also did predestinate." (Rom. viii. 29.) Thus showing our high origin, in that He did not love us now first, but from the beginning: and it is no little matter to be loved of old, and from the beginning.

Says God makes his word known in its own time through preaching, and points out that the Roman world, with a common language and open roads, was ready for the message to spread.
An apostle who preaches the word

Ver. 3. "But hath in due times manifested His word through preaching, which is committed unto me." That is, the preaching is committed unto me. For this included everything, the Gospel, and things present, and things future, life, and godliness, and faith, and all things at once.
4: Five Links in a Golden Chain
Notes that Acts never names Titus, though Paul's other letters show him as a close coworker, and takes "true son" to mean that Paul had led him to faith. The greeting wishes him grace and peace.
Titus, a true son in the faith

"To Titus mine own son," that is, my true son. For it is possible for men not to be true sons, as he of whom he says, "If any man that is called a brother be a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a railer, or a drunkard, with such an one no not to eat." (1 Cor. v. 11.) Here is a son, but not a true son. A son indeed he is, because he has once received the grace, and has been regenerated: but he is not a true son, because he is unworthy of his Father, and a deserter to the usurped sovereignty of another.

Barclay notes that Paul's custom was to appoint elders as soon as a church was founded, as in Acts 14:23, and that Crete, which Homer called the island of a hundred cities, needed leaders in each town. He refers readers to his study of the matching list in 1 Timothy 3.

"For this cause left I thee in Crete." As if the whole world had been one house, they divided it among themselves, administering its affairs everywhere, each taking care of his several portion of it. "For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are [R. V. were] wanting." He does not command this in an imperious manner; "that thou shouldest set in order," he says.

Barclay groups the positive qualities in three sets and starts with hospitality, the Greek word meaning love of strangers, which mattered in a world of costly and unsafe inns. He adds that the elder needs a firm grip on reliable teaching so as to encourage believers and answer opponents.

Ver. 8. "But a lover of hospitality, a lover of good men, sober, just, holy, temperate." Ver. 9. "Holding fast the faithful word as he has been taught." You see what intensity of virtue he required. "Not given to filthy lucre," that is, showing great contempt for money. "A lover of hospitality, a lover of good men, sober, just, holy"; he means, giving away all his substance to them that need. "Temperate"; he speaks not here of one who fasts, but of one who commands his passions, his tongue, his hands, his eyes.

Barclay opens a chapter on Christian character in action, taking people by age and station. The older men are to be sober, serious, prudent and healthy in faith, love and endurance, having learned which pleasures cost more than they are worth.

There are some failings which age has, that youth has not. Barclay notes that the Cretans were known as turbulent people impatient of authority, and he reads Paul's list as the marks of a good citizen: law-abiding, respectful of authority, ready to do good, free of slander, gentle and kind to all.

Chap. iii. 1. "Put them in mind to be subject to principalities and powers, to obey magistrates, to be ready to every good work, to speak evil of no man, to be no brawlers." Our lips should be pure from reviling. For if our reproaches are true, it is not for us to utter them, but for the Judge to enquire into the matter.

But avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions, and fights that come from the Law: for they are useless and vain. Because questions are manifold and diverse, Solomon therefore spoke about those who seek God, saying: "But those who seek him rightly have found peace" (Prov. 16:8). Those, then, who do not seek God rightly cannot find peace. There are very many examples of those who seek God not rightly. The Jews seek God perversely, hoping that they can find him without Christ.

And why he is to be avoided after a first and second reproof, he gives the reasons, saying: "that such a one is subverted, and sins, since he is condemned by himself". Ver. 12. "When I shall send Artemas unto thee, or Tychicus; be diligent to come unto me to Nicopolis." What sayest thou? After having appointed him to preside over Crete, dost thou again summon him to thyself? It was not to withdraw him from that occupation, but to discipline him the more for it. For that he does not call him to attend upon him, as if he took him everywhere with him as his follower, appears from what he adds: "For I have determined there to winter." Now Nicopolis is a city of Thrace.

Send Zenas, the teacher of the law, and Apollos ahead with care, so that nothing may be lacking to them. This is the Apollos about whom it is written to the Corinthians too: "Each of you says: I am of Paul, but I of Apollos, and I of Cephas" (1 Cor. 1:12). All who are with me greet you. Either he used the customary formula, saying that Titus was greeted by all who were with him; or else he says it properly of Titus, because he was such as to deserve the love of all who were with Paul. And it is great praise of Titus to be greeted through Paul by all. Greet those who love us in faith. If everyone who loves loved in faith, and there were not others who love without faith, Paul would never have added faith to love, saying: Greet those who love us in faith.
